prompt: What does the browser keep after reading a page's HTML?

choices.text: The HTML text, which it re-reads whenever a script asks
choices.why: It reads the text once and keeps something else.

choices.text: A tree of objects, one per element and text
choices.why: Right: the DOM.

choices.text: A picture of the page, drawn once
choices.why: The drawing follows the tree, and changes when the tree does.

choices.text: Only the elements that have an `id`
choices.why: Every element and every text became a node.

prompt: `document.body.childNodes.length` was 6 and `children.length` was 3. What were the other three?

Right.
The `head` is not inside `body`.

Right.

prompt: `data-book-id="42"` on an element. How is it read in JavaScript, and what type is the value?

choices.why: It is under `dataset`, and the value is text.
Right. It printed `42 string`.

prompt: Why does the section put `data-id` on each row rather than finding the book by its title?
hint: What changes, and what does not?

choices.text: Titles cannot be read from the DOM
choices.why: The title was read with `textContent`.
The section gives a different reason.

choices.text: Titles and positions change; an id does not
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Two books can never share a title
choices.why: They can, which is one more reason for an id.

prompt: A list of books arrives as an array of objects. Which sequence matches this lesson?

choices.text: Join the titles into one string and set it as `innerHTML`
choices.why: Data from outside belongs in `textContent`.

choices.text: Clone a template per book, fill it with `textContent`, attach them
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Set each title as a `data-` attribute on the list
choices.why: That shows nothing on the page.
It finds elements; it does not make them.
